description:
We are working on a map that combines MODIS and VIIRS satellite fire data to show fire hotspots clearly in one place. Join us if you’re interested in satellite data, maps, or climate. We’re looking for someone with any of these skills:

AI-assisted development (full-stack)

Data analysis / data visualization (preferred)

GIS or remote sensing (preferred)

Prompt engineering

Cloud infrastructure (preferred)
summary:
IGNIS is an interactive web application that brings NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS observations into a historical burning-activity calendar for study areas around Lahore, Pakistan, and California, USA. Using more than 1.5 million authentic detection records, it applies sensor-specific quality filters, aligns observations by UTC date, and integrates daily occupancy on a shared 0.02° grid.

Users can select dates, draw geographic areas, explore monthly and daily activity, compare supported historical periods, and download observations, analytics and calendar visualizations. Raw hotspot detections remain distinct from occupied cell-days; neither represents individual wildfires or burned area.

IGNIS addresses the challenge through reproducible, sensor-aware integration and accessible exploration. Calibration experiments are documented transparently: coefficients that failed seasonal or geographic validation were not applied. By preserving uncertainty and distinguishing missing records from confirmed absence, IGNIS helps researchers and land managers investigate recorded activity without overstating satellite capabilities.
details:
IGNIS is an interactive web application that helps researchers, fire managers and land managers explore historical satellite-recorded burning activity. It brings together more than 1.5 million authentic NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS observations from study areas around Lahore, Pakistan, and California, USA.

Our Python processing pipeline validates coordinates, UTC timestamps, product versions and fire classifications, applies sensor-specific quality filters, and checks for exact duplicate measurements. No exact duplicates were found in the supplied datasets. Retained observations are placed on a shared 0.02° geographic grid. Each grid cell detected by either sensor is counted once per UTC day; these daily values are summed into monthly cell-days. This provides sensor-aware integration while keeping raw detection counts separate.

Users can select a region and date range, switch between sensors, explore a month-by-year calendar, inspect daily activity, and draw or edit a geographic area. The map, metrics, historical comparisons and exports update together. Calculations use the full selected observations, rather than the sampled markers displayed on the map. Users can download analytical CSVs, selected hotspot records and calendar visualizations.

Historical comparisons match calendar periods and sensor configurations. Where sufficient eligible records exist, IGNIS calculates medians, percentile ranges and robust deviations to describe unusually high or low recorded activity. Seasonal charts help users explore recurring patterns while acknowledging unequal record support.

We developed and tested IGNIS on an HP ZBook G10 workstation, using PyCharm and OpenAI Codex for development assistance. The scientific pipeline uses Python, NumPy and pandas. The static website uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, browser workers and Leaflet. Verification uses pytest, Node.js and Playwright. No specialized satellite-processing hardware or runtime database is required.

The project’s creative contribution is combining an explorable historical calendar with geographic selection, reproducible analysis and transparent scientific interpretation. We considered sensor resolution, acquisition timing, confidence definitions, archive/NRT differences, classification uncertainty and missing observation coverage. Calibration candidates were tested but not applied when seasonal or geographic validation failed.

IGNIS supports historical research and planning. It does not treat missing detections as proof of no fire, equate hotspots with confirmed wildfires, or present cell-days as burned area. Its intended impact is to make NASA observations easier to investigate without overstating their comparability or predictive capabilities.
dataRefs: The Impact of Cloud on Active Fire Detections
